[Slides](16-text-regex-slides.html) · [Live script](16-text-regex.R) ·
[Source](https://github.com/ArielOrtizBobea/aem6850/blob/main/fall-2026/sessions/16-text-regex.qmd) ·
[the project](data/16-text-regex.zip)

How to turn text into variables with patterns and word counts. The
session starts with what a regular expression is and its metacharacters,
then the three everyday uses (validating a format, extracting a value,
replacing text) on short examples, then the same tools on a large text:
the Federal Reserve's policy statements since 2006. Two variables come out of them: the target range for the
policy rate, pulled out of each statement with a regular expression and
compared with the Fed's own daily series, and the tone of each statement,
counted with a finance word list. A chatbot writes the extraction code
here, as it often will in your own work, so the session teaches enough of
the syntax to read a pattern piece by piece and to test it on the whole
corpus.

**The project.** Install the packages once, in the R Console:
`install.packages(c("stringr", "stopwords"))`. Download
[16-text-regex.zip](data/16-text-regex.zip), unzip it, and open
`16-text-regex.Rproj`, so that R starts in the project folder. It holds:

- `fomc_statements.csv`: every policy statement of the Federal Open
  Market Committee from January 2006 to September 2026, one row each
  (date, url, words, text, scheduled).
- `fred_target_range.csv`: the Fed's target for the policy rate on every
  day, from FRED.
- `lm_words.csv`: the positive and negative word lists of Loughran and
  McDonald.
- `chat_prompt.txt`, `chat_reply.md` and `chat_reply.R`: a prompt to a
  chatbot, its full reply, and the reply's code, unchanged.
- `SOURCE.txt`: each source, its address, its terms of use and the date
  it was collected.

## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Say what a regular expression is and read its metacharacters.
- Write a pattern with character classes, quantifiers, `^`, `$` and
  `\\b`.
- Validate a format with an anchored pattern and `str_detect()`.
- Extract numbers from text with `str_extract()`, capture groups and
  `str_match()`.
- Clean and reformat text with `str_replace_all()` and backreferences.
- Give the base R name of each `stringr` function used.
- Rerun a test on strings copied from the documents after every change
  to a pattern.
- Find a word in many documents with `str_detect()`.
- Count a word in each document with `str_count()`.
- Split text into words with `str_extract_all()`.
- Count words with `table()` after dropping stop words.
- Score each statement's net tone with a finance word list.
- Read a chatbot's pattern piece by piece, including `(?: )`, lazy `.*?`
  and the options of `regex()`.
- Compare an extracted variable with FRED's daily series row by row.
- Find a look-alike character by its code point with `utf8ToInt()`.
- Replace a character in every document with `str_replace_all()`.
- Say when a regular expression is the right tool, and when a parser or a
  model is.

:::

::::: {.columns}

::: {style="font-size:0.88em; border-left: 4px solid #B31B1B; padding: 0.3em 0.9em; background: #F7F7F7;"}

The Federal Open Market Committee decided today to establish a target
range for the federal funds rate of [0&nbsp;to&nbsp;1/4&nbsp;percent]{style="background:#FFF3B0"}.

Since the Committee's last meeting, labor market conditions have
[deteriorated]{style="color:#B31B1B;font-weight:600"}, and the available
data indicate that consumer spending, business investment, and industrial
production have [declined]{style="color:#B31B1B;font-weight:600"}.
Financial markets remain quite [strained]{style="color:#B31B1B;font-weight:600"}
and credit conditions tight. Overall, the outlook for economic activity
has [weakened]{style="color:#B31B1B;font-weight:600"} further.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="48%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.9em"}

- **A pattern** finds [0&nbsp;to&nbsp;1/4&nbsp;percent]{style="background:#FFF3B0"}
  → `lower` = 0 and `upper` = 0.25 (percent).
- **A count of words on a finance word list**: the statement has 403
  words. [8 are negative]{style="color:#B31B1B;font-weight:600"} (the 4 in
  red are in these two paragraphs) and 2 are positive.
- **Net tone** = 100 × (positive − negative) / words
  =&nbsp;100&nbsp;×&nbsp;(2&nbsp;−&nbsp;8)&nbsp;/&nbsp;403&nbsp;=&nbsp;−1.49.
- Run on all 171 statements from 2006 to 2026, each method gives a column

## Three papers that count words {#papers .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.74em"}

| Paper | Text | What they counted | Finding |
|:-------------|:-------------|:----------------------|:-------------------------|
| [Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024) | articles in 10 US newspapers, each month | share of articles with a word from each of three lists: economy, policy, uncertainty (an uncertainty index) | the index rises near close elections, wars, 9/11, the failure of Lehman Brothers and the 2011 debt-ceiling fight |
| [Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdab094) | transcripts of Fed policy meetings, [2000–2011]{style="white-space:nowrap"} | negative and positive words from a finance word list | the committee aimed at about 1.5 percent inflation, below the 2 percent usually assumed |

### Baker, Bloom & Davis: a keyword index from newspapers


::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.7em"}

- [Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024)
  counted, each month, the articles in 10 large US newspapers that
  contain a word from each of three lists. The lists also take variants
  such as "uncertainties" and "the Fed". (Congress is the US
  legislature; the White House is the President's office.)
- Teams of University of Chicago students read about 12,000 randomly
  drawn articles and marked whether each discussed economic policy
  uncertainty. Their verdicts chose the policy words and tested the
  count.
- **Keyword index**: the share of documents in each period that contain
  chosen words.
- **Finding.** The index rises near close presidential elections, the
  Gulf Wars (1991 and 2003, both in Iraq), 9/11, the failure of Lehman
  Brothers (a large US investment bank, September 2008), and the 2011
  dispute in Congress over the legal limit on federal borrowing.
- **Takeaway:** a widely used index is a count of documents matching
  three word lists, and people reading a sample by hand gave it
  credibility.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/16-text-regex/D02-epu-keyword-index.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Three word lists joined by AND: economy (economic, economy), uncertainty (uncertain, uncertainty) and policy (Congress, deficit, Federal Reserve, legislation, regulation, White House). An article counts if it has a word from each list; the monthly share of such articles in 10 newspapers, scaled and averaged, is the index."}

[The index, monthly, January 1985 to September 2026: Baker, Bloom & Davis,
policyuncertainty.com.]{.source}

:::

:::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The scaling: divide by all articles in that paper and month, standardize
each paper's series, average the 10, set the mean to 100 (section 2.1 of
NBER WP 21633). The list of the 10 papers is on policyuncertainty.com.
:::

:::


### Shapiro & Wilson: the tone of Fed meetings


::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.7em"}

- **Transcript**: a lightly edited word-for-word record of an FOMC
  meeting, released after five years.
- **Word list (dictionary)**: a fixed list of words tied to a category,
  such as negative words.
- [Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdab094)
  counted the negative and positive words on the lists of
  [Loughran & McDonald (JF, 2011)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01625.x)
  in what each speaker said at each meeting. 14 research assistants
  scored 182 randomly drawn texts, and the word score agreed with them
  far better than a general-purpose list did.
- They related negative tone to the staff's inflation forecast at each
  meeting. Negativity was lowest near 1.5 percent inflation.
- **Finding.** Over 2000–2011 the committee aimed at about 1.5 percent
  inflation, below the 2 percent usually assumed. The Fed first announced
  a 2 percent goal in January 2012.
- **Takeaway:** a word count on Fed text estimated the inflation goal the
  committee worked to before it announced one, once people's scores on a
  random sample backed the count.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/16-text-regex/D03-fed-tone-flow.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Four steps: FOMC meeting transcripts from 2000 to 2011; counts of negative and positive words from a finance word list, ignoring words after not; 14 research assistants' scores of 182 random texts, rank correlation 0.40 against 0.14 for a general list; negative tone related to the staff's inflation forecast, least negative near 1.5 percent."}

:::

:::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The method details (14 research assistants, 182 scores on a 1 to 5 scale,
rank correlation 0.40 against 0.14 for the Harvard General Inquirer,
words after "not" ignored) are from the FRBSF working paper version
(2019-02, January 2021). The published abstract gives about 1.5 percent
over 2000-11.
:::

:::


### Djourelova: one phrase in the news


::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- The Associated Press (AP) is a US news agency. Many local papers
  reprint its stories, called AP copy. Its style guide, the wording rules
  its reporters follow, dropped "illegal immigrant" in April 2013.
- [Djourelova (AER, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20211537) counted
  the phrase in more than 2,000 US print and online outlets. In outlets
  that relied on AP copy, articles using it fell by 28% compared with
  other outlets.
- She linked answers to a large US election survey to the AP reliance of
  the newspapers sold in each respondent's county.
- **Finding.** Readers exposed to the change through local media
  supported restrictive immigration policy less.
- **Takeaway:** an exact phrase count works when the wording itself is
  what you study.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

![](figures/16-text-regex/D04-ap-style-timeline.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="A timeline with one marker in April 2013, when the AP style guide dropped 'illegal immigrant'. After it, articles using the phrase fell 28 percent in outlets that rely on AP copy, and readers in counties whose papers rely on AP supported restrictive immigration policy less."}

:::

:::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The counts (more than 2,000 outlets, 28 percent, the CCES survey) are from
the May 2020 working paper version. The AER abstract confirms the finding
on readers.
:::

# 2 · Regex basics {#part-regex}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

:::

## What a regular expression is {#what-regex .smaller .code-120}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.78em"}

- A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern, written as a string,
  that describes a set of texts. A function reads the pattern and finds
  the stretches of text that fit it, called **matches**.
- Most characters match themselves: the pattern `"rate"` finds the
  letters r, a, t, e in that order. These are **literals**.
- A few characters have a special meaning, such as `?`, which makes the
  piece before it optional. These are **metacharacters**.
- The same syntax works in most programming languages and text editors.

:::

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
# install.packages(c("stringr", "stopwords"))   # once
library(stringr)               # text functions; every name starts with str_
words <- c("color", "colour", "colr", "Colour")
str_detect(words, "colou?r")   # TRUE if the string contains a match; ? makes the u optional
str_view(words, "colou?r")     # the strings that match, each match in < >
str_detect(words, regex("colou?r", ignore_case = TRUE))   # upper and lower case match alike
```

::: {style="font-size:0.74em"}

Matching is case-sensitive, so "Colour" does not match until
`ignore_case = TRUE` inside `regex()` turns that off.

:::

## Metacharacters {#metacharacters .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

| Symbol | Means | Pattern | Example match |
|:------|:------------------------------------|:------------|:--------------|
| `.` | any one character | `r.te` | rate, rite |
| `[ ]` | one character from the set | `[0-9]` | 4 |
| `[^ ]` | one character not in the set | `[^0-9]` | the - and / in 4-3/4 |
| `?` | the piece before, zero or one time | `rates?` | rate, rates |
| `*` | the piece before, zero or more times | `10*` | 1, 10, 100 |
| `+` | the piece before, one or more times | `[0-9]+` | 2026 |
| `{n}` | the piece before, exactly n times | `[0-9]{4}` | 2026 |
| `^` `$` | the start, the end of the text | `^The` | "The" at the start |
| <code>&#124;</code> | the piece on either side | <code>raise&#124;lower</code> | raise, lower |
| `( )` | a group, whose match R can return alone | `([0-9]+)%` | 4% (group: 4) |
| `\\` | the next character is plain (in R, typed twice) | `\\.` | a period |

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

**Shortcuts**: `\\d` a digit, `\\s` a space or line break, `\\w` a letter,
digit or underscore, `\\b` the edge of a word. In R each backslash is
written twice: you type `"\\d"` and the pattern receives `\d`. A
**piece** is one character, a class in brackets, or a group.

:::

## Character classes `[ ]` and `\\d` {#classes .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
# a sentence from the Fed's policy statement of 22 March 2023
x <- "the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent."
str_view(x, "\\d")
str_view(x, "[0-9/-]")
str_view(x, "[^a-z ]")      # ^ inside brackets: any character NOT in the set
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Character class**: characters in brackets. It matches any one of them.
- Inside brackets, `0-9` means any digit and `a-z` any lowercase letter.
  A hyphen placed last, as in `[0-9/-]`, is a plain hyphen.
- `[^ ]` matches any one character NOT in the set. The set in `[^a-z ]`
  is the lowercase letters and the space, so it catches the capital C,
  the digits, the - and the /, and the final period.
- **`\\d`**: one digit, the same as `[0-9]`.
- The Fed writes rates as a whole number and a fraction: "4-3/4 percent"
  is 4.75 percent.

:::

## The dot and the escape {#dot .smaller .code-110}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr and x"
str_view(c("rate", "rite", "r8te", "rte"), "r.te")   # . : any one character
str_view(x, "\\.")           # \\. : a period
c(str_count(x, "."), str_count(x, "\\."))
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.78em"}

- **The dot `.`**: any one character.
- The dot needs exactly one character, so "rte" does not match.
  `str_count()` counts the matches in each string.
- **Escape**: a backslash that turns a metacharacter back into a plain
  character: `\\.` a period, `\\$` a dollar sign, `\\?` a question mark,
  `\\(` a parenthesis.
- `x` has 97 characters. `"."` matches each of them, and `"\\."` only the
  period.

:::

## Quantifiers {#quantifiers .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs x"
str_extract_all(x, "[0-9/-]+")            # + : one or more of the piece before
str_extract(x, "\\d+-\\d+/\\d+")           # a whole number, a hyphen, a fraction
str_detect(c("1/4 percentage point", "1/2 percentage points"), "percentage points?")
str_extract(c("year 2026", "26"), "\\d{4}")   # {4} : exactly four digits
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Quantifier**: a mark after a piece (one character, a class in
  brackets, or a group) saying how many times it may repeat: `+` one or
  more, `*` zero or more, `?` zero or one, `{4}` exactly four.
- `str_extract()` returns the first match in each string, or NA.
  `str_extract_all()` returns every match, as a list with one element per
  string (the `[[1]]`).

:::

## Anchors and word boundaries {#anchors-words .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
s <- c("rate", "the rate rose", "moderate", "rates")
str_detect(s, "rate")             # the literal also matches inside other words
str_detect(s, "\\brate\\b")       # \\b : the edge of a word
str_detect(s, "^rate$")           # ^ : start of the text; $ : end of the text
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Anchor**: `^` pins the pattern to the start of the text and `$` to
  the end. With both, the whole string must match. Inside brackets, `^`
  means NOT.
- **Word boundary `\\b`**: the edge between a letter, digit or underscore
  and anything else: a space, a punctuation mark, or the start or end of
  the text.
- **False positive**: text the pattern catches but should skip, such as
  "moderate" when you want the word "rate". **False negative**: text it
  misses but should catch, such as "rates" under `\\brate\\b`.

:::

## Capture groups `( )` {#groups .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
rates <- c("4-3/4", "1-1/2", "5")             # rates as the Fed writes them
m <- str_match(rates, "(\\d+)-(\\d+)/(\\d+)")  # whole number, numerator, denominator
m
as.numeric(m[, 2]) + as.numeric(m[, 3]) / as.numeric(m[, 4])   # 4 + 3/4 = 4.75
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Capture group**: a part of the pattern inside `( )`. `str_match()`
  returns the whole match in column 1, then one column per group, in the
  order the groups open.
- The groups split "4-3/4" into 4, 3 and 4, so the last line can compute
  4 + 3/4 = 4.75.
- "5" has no fraction, so the pattern finds no match and the whole row is
  NA.

:::

## Alternatives `|` {#alternatives .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
# phrases from the Fed statements of 8 Aug 2006, 22 Mar 2023 and 16 Dec 2008
phrases <- c("keep its target for the federal funds rate at 5-1/4 percent",
             "raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent",
             "establish a target range for the federal funds rate of 0 to 1/4 percent")
str_match(phrases, "(?:at|to|of) ([0-9/-]+) percent")
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- `at|to|of` matches at, to or of. `(?: )` groups the three words without
  adding a column, so the number lands in column 2.
- Rows 2 and 3 return only the upper end of the range:
  - The pattern needs a space and "percent" right after the number.
  - After "to 4-3/4" comes "to 5", so the search moves on and matches
    "to 5 percent".
  - Getting both ends takes a second number group.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The same constructions come back in the chatbot's pattern in Part 5.
:::

# 3 · Validation, extraction and replacement {#part-uses}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- The functions for each task
- Validating a format
- Extracting numbers
- Replacing and cleaning text
- Testing a pattern
- Exercise 1

:::

## The functions for each task {#functions .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}

| Task and result | `stringr` | base R |
|:---------------------|:------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|
| **find, validate**<br>TRUE or FALSE | `str_detect(x, p)` | `grepl(p, x)` |
| **count**<br>a number per string | `str_count(x, p)` | `lengths(regmatches(x, gregexpr(p, x)))` |
| **extract**<br>first match, or NA | `str_extract(x, p)` | `regmatches(x, regexpr(p, x))` |
| **groups**<br>match, then groups | `str_match(x, p)` | `regmatches(x, regexec(p, x))` |
| **extract all**<br>a list of matches | `str_extract_all(x, p)` | `regmatches(x, gregexpr(p, x))` |
| **replace**<br>the new strings | `str_replace_all(x, p, r)` | `gsub(p, r, x)` |

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.72em"}

Result: what the `stringr` function returns. `x` is the text, `p` the
pattern and `r` the replacement. Base R puts the pattern first, and its
extract functions drop strings with no match. Chatbots write either style.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Where base R and `stringr` behave differently:

| `stringr` | base R | What differs |
|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------|:---------------------------|
| `str_extract(x, p)` | `regmatches(x, regexpr(p, x))` | base R drops strings with no match, so the result is shorter than `x` |
| `str_match(x, p)` | `regmatches(x, regexec(p, x))` | a list, not a matrix; an optional group that did not match is `""`, not NA |
| `str_split(x, p)` | `strsplit(x, p)` | `strsplit()` drops a final empty string |
| `str_c(...)` | `paste0(...)` | `paste0()` writes NA as "NA"; `str_c()` returns NA |
| `regex(p, ignore_case = TRUE)` | `ignore.case = TRUE` | |

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

**Engine**: the code that runs a pattern. Base R has two, and
`perl = TRUE` picks the second.

The other functions used today:

| `stringr` | base R |
|:--|:--|
| `str_split(x, p)` | `strsplit(x, p)` |
| `str_sub(x, 1, 4)` | `substr(x, 1, 4)` |
| `str_to_lower(x)` | `tolower(x)` |

On all 171 statements, the `grepl()` and `gregexpr()` counts equal the
`stringr` results with or without `perl = TRUE`. The two engines differ on
the dot: the default engine's `.` matches a line break, which `stringr`'s
does only with `dotall = TRUE`; with `perl = TRUE`, `.` stops at a line
break unless the pattern starts with `(?s)`. So the reply's first step,
run through `regexpr()`, gives 23 NA with the default engine (the same as
`stringr` with `dotall`) and 36 with `perl = TRUE`. `perl = TRUE` also
adds lookarounds such as `(?=...)`. The three changes written in base R
give 170 of 171 with either engine (Practice 5).

:::

## Validating a format {#validation .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
fips <- c("06037", "6037", "36109", "3610A", " 36109")   # US county codes
str_detect(fips, "^\\d{5}$")         # exactly five digits, nothing before or after
str_detect(fips, "\\d{5}")           # without the anchors, " 36109" passes
fips[!str_detect(fips, "^\\d{5}$")]  # the values that fail
dates <- c("2026-10-22", "10/22/2026", "2026-1-5")
str_detect(dates, "^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$")   # year-month-day, two digits each
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Validation**: checking that every value has the format it should,
  before you merge or analyze the data.
- A **FIPS code** is the US government's five-digit code for each US
  county: two digits for the state, three for the county. Read as a
  number, "06037" (Los Angeles County, California) becomes 6037, and a
  merge on it fails.

:::

## Extracting numbers {#extraction .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
prices <- c("$1,250", "price: $99.99", "free", "$52,000")
str_extract(prices, "[0-9,.]+")             # digits, commas and periods
ages <- c("<1", "1-5", "5-10", "15+")        # age groups in a mortality table
str_match(ages, "(\\d+)(?:-(\\d+))?")         # group 1: the first number; group 2: the second
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Extraction**: keeping only the part of each string that matches.
- `str_extract()` returns the match as text.
- `str_match()` returns one column per group, so "5-10" splits into "5"
  and "10". `(?:-(\\d+))?` makes the hyphen and the second number optional
  together; when they are missing, group 2 is NA.
- The pattern returns 1 for "<1" and 15 for "15+". You code by hand that
  "<1" starts at 0 and that "15+" has no upper end.

:::

## Replacing and cleaning text {#replacement .smaller .code-110}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs prices"
amount <- str_extract(prices, "[0-9,.]+")       # "free" has no digits, so NA
as.numeric(str_replace_all(amount, ",", ""))    # drop the commas, then convert
str_squish("  Federal   Reserve \n Board ")     # \n: a line break; result: one space between words
# month/day/year becomes year-month-day
str_replace(c("10/22/2026", "01/05/2026"), "(\\d{2})/(\\d{2})/(\\d{4})", "\\3-\\1-\\2")
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- **Replacement**: rewriting what the pattern matches. `str_replace()`
  changes the first match, `str_replace_all()` every match.
- **Backreference**: `\\1`, `\\2` and `\\3` in the replacement stand for
  what groups 1, 2 and 3 matched. The US writes dates month/day/year
  (10/22/2026), so the replacement puts the year first: 2026-10-22.
- `as.numeric("1,250")` gives NA, which is why the commas go first.

:::

## Testing a pattern {#tests .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
should_match <- c("the federal funds rate", "longer-term interest rates")
should_skip  <- c("at a moderate pace", "to generate sustained improvement")
str_detect(should_match, "\\brate\\b")
str_detect(should_skip, "\\brate\\b")
str_detect(should_match, "\\brates?\\b")      # ? makes the "s" optional
str_detect(should_skip, "\\brates?\\b")
str_detect(should_skip, "rate")               # without \\b, "moderate" and "generate" match
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- Test a pattern on strings with a known answer first. Goal here: the
  word "rate" or "rates", and not "moderate" or "generate".
- **Should-match and should-skip tests**: short vectors of real strings
  the pattern must catch and must leave alone, rerun after every change.
- `\\brate\\b` misses "rates" (false negative); `"rate"` catches both skip
  strings (false positives); `\\brates?\\b` passes both.
- Copy test strings from the documents. When the corpus shows a case the
  pattern gets wrong, add that string to one of the two vectors.

:::

## Exercise 1 {#exercise-1 .smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Exercise

::: {style="font-size:1.2em"}

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1
#| exercise: true
#| script: "Exercise 1 (5 minutes)"
#| eval: false
# Exercise 1 (5 minutes). R Console; needs stringr. Answers to a survey
# question on yearly income:
income <- c("$52,000", "48500", "Income: $61,250.00", "N/A", "about 40k",
            "$1,000,000")
# 1. Validation: write ok_pat, a pattern for an answer that is only an
#    amount: an optional $, then digits and commas, then optional cents
#    (.00). Run str_detect(income, ok_pat). Alone, $ means the end of the
#    text, so write \\$ for a dollar sign.
# 2. Extraction: pull the number out of every answer with str_extract().
# 3. Replacement: drop the commas with str_replace_all(), then as.numeric().
# 4. Read the result next to income. Which answers give NA or a wrong number?
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: how many answers pass step 1, and
# what "about 40k" becomes.
```

:::

### Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise-1-solution
#| purl: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr"
income <- c("$52,000", "48500", "Income: $61,250.00", "N/A", "about 40k",
            "$1,000,000")
ok_pat <- "^\\$?[0-9,]+(\\.\\d{2})?$"
str_detect(income, ok_pat)
n <- str_extract(income, "[0-9,.]+")
as.numeric(str_replace_all(n, ",", ""))
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

**Three answers pass: "\$52,000", "48500" and "\$1,000,000". "about 40k"
becomes 40, a thousand times too small, with no warning. It fails step 1,
which is how you find it.**

:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Uses only the functions of this part. The $ needs an escape because, on
its own, $ is the end anchor. Without ^ and $, "Income: $61,250.00" passes
step 1. "N/A" gives NA in step 2, which is the right answer for a missing
value.
:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- The Fed's policy statements

Unzip [16-text-regex.zip](data/16-text-regex.zip) (the 171 statements in
`fomc_statements.csv`, plus the files for later slides) and open

## The Fed's policy statements {#statement .smaller}

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="48%"}

![](figures/16-text-regex/S01-statement-20230322-top.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The third paragraph of the Federal Reserve's statement of 22 March 2023, as the Fed's page shows it, with the sentence 'the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent' highlighted."}

:::

::: {.column width="52%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.82em"}

- The Federal Reserve ("the Fed") is the US central bank.
- Its **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)** sets the policy interest
  rate. It meets eight times a year and publishes a statement after each
  meeting. A few statements follow unscheduled meetings.
- The **federal funds rate** is the rate banks charge each other for
  overnight loans. The Fed steers it.
- The **target range** is the band the FOMC announces for that rate.
  "4-3/4 to 5 percent" means 4.75 to 5. Before 16 December 2008 the FOMC
  announced a single number.
- **The file** `fomc_statements.csv` has one row per statement: 171
  statements, 31 Jan 2006 to 16 Sep 2026, 165 of them after scheduled
  meetings.

:::

:::

:::::

[Screenshot: federalreserve.gov, statement of 22 March 2023 (public domain).]{.source}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
This is the file the scraping session built. The meeting came 12 days
after Silicon Valley Bank failed, which is why paragraph 2 opens "The U.S.
banking system is sound and resilient."
:::

:::

## Finding a word in 171 statements {#detect .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console, in the 16-text-regex folder; needs stringr; reads fomc_statements.csv (date, url, words, text, scheduled)"
fomc <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")
dim(fomc)
c(inflation = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "inflation")),
  Inflation = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "Inflation")),
  either    = sum(str_detect(fomc$text, regex("inflation", ignore_case = TRUE))))
fomc$n_infl <- str_count(fomc$text, regex("inflation", ignore_case = TRUE))
summary(fomc$n_infl)
fomc$date[which(fomc$n_infl == 0)]   # which(): the positions where the condition is TRUE
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- **Literal pattern**: a pattern with no metacharacters. Matching is
  case-sensitive: 165 statements contain "inflation", 99 "Inflation", 168
  either.
- `str_detect()` gives TRUE or FALSE per statement, and `sum()` counts the
  TRUEs. `str_count()` gives the number of matches per statement, a new
  column `n_infl` (0 to 17, median 8).
- The three statements without "inflation" all followed unscheduled
  meetings: 17 Aug 2007, and 3 and 23 Mar 2020, as the coronavirus
  spread.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Paragraphs inside `text` are separated by a blank line ("\n\n"). The
three statements with no "inflation" are the unscheduled 17 Aug 2007 and
23 Mar 2020 and the emergency cut of 3 Mar 2020.
:::

:::

## False positives in a large text {#false-positives .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc"
sum(str_count(fomc$text, "rate"))
sum(str_count(fomc$text, "\\brate\\b"))
caught <- unlist(str_extract_all(fomc$text, "[a-z]*rate[a-z]*"))   # every word containing "rate"
head(sort(table(caught), decreasing = TRUE), 6)
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.74em"}

- The literal "rate" matches 982 times, the whole word 705 times. The
  other 277 are 58 "rates", which you may want (`\\brates?\\b` keeps them),
  and 219 inside other words, such as "moderate" (144).
- A false positive is text the pattern catches but should skip. In a
  short test vector you see one at a glance. In 171 statements, a table of
  everything the pattern caught shows them.
- `unlist()` puts every statement's matches in one vector, so `table()`
  can count them.

:::

## Splitting text into words {#tokens .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs stringr and fomc"
i <- which(fomc$date == "2023-03-22")                         # the row of the 22 Mar 2023 statement
fomc$year <- as.numeric(str_sub(fomc$date, 1, 4))             # the year, used in Exercise 2
tokens <- str_extract_all(str_to_lower(fomc$text), "[a-z]+")  # every run of letters
head(tokens[[i]], 12)
length(tokens[[i]])
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.74em"}

- **Token**: one unit of text after splitting, here a word in lower case.
  Extracting every run of letters does the split: spaces, punctuation and
  numbers are left out.
- `str_to_lower()` comes first so "Inflation" and "inflation" count as
  one word. `tokens` is a list with one vector of words per statement,
  and `[[i]]` picks one.
- The apostrophe is not a letter, so "Committee's" becomes two tokens,
  "committee" and "s".

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The file's `words` column says 365 for this statement. It counts words
differently, which is why the slides say tokens.
:::

:::

## Word counts and stop words {#stop-words .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs tokens and the stopwords package"
all_words <- unlist(tokens)
length(all_words)
head(sort(table(all_words), decreasing = TRUE), 8)
stop_words <- stopwords::stopwords("en")     # pkg::fun(): a package's function without library()
kept <- all_words[!all_words %in% stop_words & nchar(all_words) > 1]   # !x %in% y: x is not in y
head(sort(table(kept), decreasing = TRUE), 8)
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.74em"}

- **Stop words**: very common words dropped before counting ("the", "of",
  "will"). The package's default English list (Snowball) has 175.
- **Term frequency**: a word's count divided by all tokens. "inflation" is
  1,330 of 73,839, or 1.8 percent.
- `nchar()` counts characters. `nchar(all_words) > 1` drops 1,793 more
  one-letter tokens: the s of "Committee's" and "U.S.", and middle
  initials such as the H in Jerome H. Powell (each statement ends by
  naming the members who voted).
- The stop list also drops "not" and "no", which reverse a sentence, and
  "against", which is on the negative word list used for tone.

:::

## Exercise 2 {#exercise-2 .smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Exercise

::: {style="font-size:1.3em"}

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2
#| exercise: true
#| script: "Exercise 2 (5 minutes)"
#| eval: false
# Exercise 2 (5 minutes). R Console; needs fomc (with its year column) and
# tokens from the previous slides.
# Which words appear in the statements for the first time in 2022?
#
# 1. Put the words of the 2022 statements in one vector:
#      w22 <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year == 2022])
# 2. Put the words of every statement before 2022 in a second vector
#    called before.
# 3. Keep the 2022 words that are not in the vector before (use %in% and !).
# 4. Count them with table() and sort them, largest first.
#
# Two answers to compare with the room: the most frequent new word, and the
# new words that are people's names.
```

:::

### Solution

```{r}
#| label: exercise-2-solution
#| purl: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc and tokens"
w22    <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year == 2022])
before <- unlist(tokens[fomc$year < 2022])
new    <- w22[!w22 %in% before]
head(sort(table(new), decreasing = TRUE), 16)
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

**"war" (8), then "russia" and "ukraine" (7 each) and "invasion" (6): from
16 Mar 2022 the statements say "The invasion of Ukraine by Russia is
causing tremendous human and economic hardship." The names belong to four
new voting members of the committee (Lisa D. Cook, Philip N. Jefferson,
Michael S. Barr, Susan M. Collins); d and n are their middle initials.**

:::

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Each statement lists the members who voted. Lisa D. Cook and Philip N.
Jefferson appear from 15 Jun 2022, Michael S. Barr and Susan M. Collins
from 27 Jul 2022; "d" and "n" are middle initials. Of the 2,886 words in
the 2022 statements, 105 are new, 27 different words. The exercise needs
no stop words, so a student whose stopwords install failed can still do
it.
:::

:::

## A finance word list {#lm .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; reads lm_words.csv"
lm_words <- read.csv("lm_words.csv")         # word, list: "positive" or "negative"; lower case
table(lm_words$list)
pos <- lm_words$word[lm_words$list == "positive"]
neg <- lm_words$word[lm_words$list == "negative"]
c("liability", "tax", "cost") %in% neg      # three words a general-purpose list calls negative
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- **Word list (dictionary)**: a fixed list of words tied to a category.
  Counting the words on a positive and a negative list gives a statement's
  tone.
- [Loughran & McDonald (JF, 2011)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01625.x)
  built the lists for 10-Ks, the yearly report every listed US company
  files with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the US regulator of
  stock markets).
- **Finding.** In 10-Ks from 1994 to 2008, a general-purpose list (the
  Harvard General Inquirer, built for psychology and sociology) flagged
  many words as negative. Almost three-fourths of them, such as tax, cost
  and liability, are not negative in financial text.
- **Takeaway:** a word list built for one kind of text misreads another.
  [Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdab094)
  used these lists on the Fed's meeting transcripts, and the next slides
  apply them to the statements.

:::

[Free for use in academic research; commercial licences from the authors
(sraf.nd.edu).]{.source}

## Net tone of each statement {#net-tone .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}

**Net tone**: positive words minus negative words, per 100 tokens.

:::

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc, tokens, pos and neg"
net_tone <- function(w) 100 * (sum(w %in% pos) - sum(w %in% neg)) / length(w)
j <- which(fomc$date == "2008-12-16")
w <- tokens[[j]]
w[w %in% neg]
w[w %in% pos]
net_tone(w)
fomc$tone <- sapply(tokens, net_tone)        # sapply(): the function on each statement's words
fomc[c(which.min(fomc$tone), which.max(fomc$tone)), c("date", "tone")]   # lowest, highest
```

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}

On 16 Dec 2008, during the financial crisis, the committee cut its
target to a range of 0 to 1/4 percent; the statement has 403 tokens. The
two positive words come from set phrases: "price stability" and
"exceptionally low".

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The lowest, 16 Sep 2008, came the day after Lehman Brothers filed for
bankruptcy. Its 220 tokens contain 1 positive and 7 negative words.
:::

:::

## Drawing net tone over time {#fig-tone .smaller .code-120}

```{r}
#| label: fig-tone-time
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc with its tone column"
#| fig-show: hide
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.4
par(mar = c(2.5, 4.5, 0.8, 0.5))               # margins in lines: bottom, left, top, right
plot(as.Date(fomc$date), fomc$tone, type = "h", ylim = c(-3.4, 2.8),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Net tone per 100 tokens", las = 1)    # "h": one bar per statement
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
lab <- which(fomc$date %in% c("2008-09-16", "2020-03-03", "2021-07-28"))
text(as.Date(fomc$date[lab]), fomc$tone[lab], c("16 Sep 2008", "3 Mar 2020", "28 Jul 2021"),
     pos = c(1, 3, 3), cex = 1, xpd = NA)
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- `type = "h"` draws one vertical bar from 0 to each statement's tone.
- `text()` labels three statements: the lowest (16 Sep 2008), the highest
  (28 Jul 2021) and 3 Mar 2020, a rate cut between scheduled meetings.
- `pos = 1` puts a label below its bar and `pos = 3` above it. `xpd = NA`
  lets a label run outside the box.

# 5 · A chatbot writes the extraction code {#part-chatbot}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

The task: pull the target range for the federal funds rate (lower and
upper limit, in percent) out of each of the 171 statements, with code a
chatbot wrote.

:::

- The prompt and the reply
- Reading its pattern piece by piece
- The reply's tests on 171 statements
- Comparing it with FRED, the Fed's daily series of the target
- Where the reply's code fails
- Two hyphens that look the same
- Fixing the code

:::

## The prompt and the reply {#prompt-reply .smaller}

::: {.prompt style="font-size:0.74em; border-left: 4px solid #B31B1B; padding: 0.2em 0.8em; background: #F7F7F7;"}

I have a data frame in R called fomc with a column text that holds the
full text of every FOMC statement since 2006, one statement per row. Each
statement says what the Fed decided about its policy rate, for example:
"the Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds
rate to 4-3/4 to 5 percent." Write R code with stringr that extracts the
target range from each statement into two numeric columns, lower and
upper (here 4.75 and 5).

:::

```{.r filename="chat_reply.R in the zip: steps 1 to 3 of the reply's code, unchanged; the lines above them define num and to_num()"}
# 1. Isolate the part of the statement describing the decision on the funds rate
seg <- str_extract(
  fomc$text,
  regex("decided.*?federal funds rate.*?percent\\b", ignore_case = TRUE, dotall = TRUE)
)
# 2. Pull out "to/at/of X [to Y] percent"
pat <- str_c("\\b(?:to|at|of)\\s+(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b")
m   <- str_match(seg, pat)
# 3. Convert to numeric
first  <- to_num(m[, 2])
second <- to_num(m[, 3])
fomc$lower <- first
fomc$upper <- ifelse(is.na(second), first, second)
```

::: {style="font-size:0.66em"}

The reply: "For your example, `"...to 4-3/4 to 5 percent."` gives
`lower = 4.75` and `upper = 5`." The prompt shows one example sentence and
gives no other statements to test the code on. What follows reads `num`,
step 1 and step 2 in turn. The full reply is on the session page.

:::

[Reply from Claude (claude-sonnet-5-5) through Anthropic's API, 20 October
2026, to the prompt shown. The same prompt in the chat at claude.ai can
return different code.]{.source}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
This is the chatbot the course recommended. Students will get different
code if they paste the prompt; the steps that follow apply to any reply.
:::


## Reading the number pattern {#num .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console, in the 16-text-regex folder; needs stringr and fomc"
source("chat_reply.R")      # runs the reply's code, unchanged
str_view(c("5", "1/4", "4-3/4", "0.25"), num)
to_num(c("4-3/4", "1/4", "5", "0"))
```

![](figures/16-text-regex/D06-num-pattern.png){width="94%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The pattern num split into three pieces: backslash d plus, one or more digits; an optional group of a period and digits, as in .25; an optional group of either -3/4 or /4."}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.66em"}

- **`num`**: the reply's pattern for one number as the Fed writes it
  ("5", "1/4", "4-3/4"). Step 2 uses it twice, for the lower and the
  upper limit.
- **`source()`** runs every line of a script file. `chat_reply.R` defines
  `num`, `to_num()`, `seg` and `pat`, and adds `lower` and `upper` to
  `fomc`.
- **Known-answer test**: inputs whose right output you know before
  running. In `str_view()` all four strings match in full, and `to_num()`
  returns 4.75, 0.25, 5 and 0, as expected.
- `to_num()` (in `chat_reply.R`) splits "4-3/4" into 4, 3 and 4 and
  returns 4 + 3/4.

:::

## Greedy and lazy matching {#greedy-lazy .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc and seg from chat_reply.R"
i <- which(fomc$date == "2023-03-22")
greedy <- str_extract(fomc$text[i], regex("decided.*percent", dotall = TRUE))
lazy   <- str_extract(fomc$text[i], regex("decided.*?percent", dotall = TRUE))
c(nchar(greedy), nchar(lazy))       # nchar() counts characters
lazy
identical(lazy, seg[i])             # the reply's step 1 gives the same text
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- Step 1 of the reply cuts the decision sentence out of each statement
  with lazy `.*?`.
- **Greedy `.*`** takes as many characters as it can. Here greedy runs 926
  characters, to the last "percent" in the statement ("...returning
  inflation to its 2 percent").
- **Lazy `.*?`** takes as few as it can.
- **`dotall = TRUE`** lets `.` match a line break ("\\n"). Paragraphs in
  `text` are separated by line breaks, so with dotall a match can run from
  one paragraph into the next.
- Why the reply stops at the first "percent" after "federal funds rate":
  "This keeps it from picking up other numbers in the statement, such as
  the 2 percent inflation goal, '25 basis points', or the discount rate."
  A basis point is 0.01 percentage point; the discount rate is the rate
  the Fed charges banks that borrow from it.

:::

## Reading the range pattern {#range-pattern .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs seg, pat and i"
str_match(seg[i], pat)              # the reply's step 2
```

![](figures/16-text-regex/D07-range-pattern.png){width="96%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The text 'to 4-3/4 to 5 percent' above the four pieces of the reply's pattern: to, at or of then spaces; group 1, the lower limit; an optional ' to ' with group 2, the upper limit; and percent as a whole word."}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- **`str_c()`** joins strings end to end (base R `paste0()`). `pat` pastes
  in `num`, the previous slide's number pattern, once per limit.
- On 22 March 2023, group 1 is "4-3/4" (the lower limit) and group 2 is
  "5" (the upper). `to_num()` turns them into 4.75 and 5.
- The second group is optional. A single target such as "at 5-1/4
  percent", the form used before December 2008, also matches, and the
  reply then sets upper equal to lower.

:::

## The reply's tests on 171 statements {#reply-all .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc after source(\"chat_reply.R\")"
sum(is.na(fomc$upper))                         # the reply's test 1 prints these rows; here we count them
summary(fomc[, c("lower", "upper")])           # the reply's test 2
sum(fomc$lower > fomc$upper, na.rm = TRUE)     # the reply's test 3: lower <= upper
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.7em"}

- The reply suggests three tests: print the NA rows
  (`fomc[is.na(fomc$upper), "text"]`), run `summary()`, and verify
  `lower <= upper`.
- It expects NA only for "a few unscheduled statements about liquidity
  facilities". There are 32, and reading them shows wordings the pattern
  misses.
- `summary()` shows values from 0 to 5.5 percent, all plausible for a
  policy rate, and no row has lower above upper.
- The tests cannot say whether the other 139 values are right.

:::

## Comparing with FRED {#fred .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc after the reply's code; reads fred_target_range.csv"
fred <- read.csv("fred_target_range.csv")                # date, lower, upper: one row per day
k <- match(as.Date(fomc$date) + 1, as.Date(fred$date))    # + 1: the day after each statement
fomc$fred_lower <- fred$lower[k]
fomc$fred_upper <- fred$upper[k]
fomc$agree <- fomc$lower == fomc$fred_lower & fomc$upper == fomc$fred_upper
table(fomc$agree, useNA = "ifany")
fomc$date[which(!fomc$agree)]
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.66em"}

- **FRED**, the free data service of the Federal Reserve Bank of St.
  Louis, gives the target for every day: DFEDTAR, the single target to
  15 Dec 2008 (copied into both columns), then DFEDTARL and DFEDTARU, the
  lower and upper limits.
- **`match()`** finds the position of each statement's next day among
  FRED's dates. Adding 1 to a date gives the next day. Since 2017 a new
  range takes effect the day after the statement, so the next day is the
  first day FRED shows it.
- `agree` is TRUE for 130 statements (both limits equal FRED's), FALSE
  for 9 and NA for 32 (no number found). `which()` skips NA, so only the
  nine wrong statements print. In all nine, lower equals upper, so the
  reply's lower <= upper test passes on every one.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
Since March 2017 a new range takes effect, and appears in FRED, the day
after the statement (30 changes). From 2006 to 2016 FRED shows it from the
statement date (16 changes). On the statement date itself 106 agree.
:::

:::

## Where the reply's code fails {#why-41 .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.6em"}

| What the statement says | Count | Dates | Code returns |
|:-----------------------------------------------|-----:|:-----------------------------|:------------------|
| "will maintain the target range ... at 0 to 1/4 percent": no "decided", which step 1 needs | 13 | 18&nbsp;Mar&nbsp;2009 to 21&nbsp;Sep&nbsp;2010 | NA |
| "reaffirmed its view that the current 0 to 1/4 percent target range ..." | 8 | 17&nbsp;Dec&nbsp;2014 to 28&nbsp;Oct&nbsp;2015 | NA |
| the range only in the instruction to the New York Fed (a regional Fed bank) | 1 | 23&nbsp;Mar&nbsp;2020 | NA |
| no target stated | 1 | 17&nbsp;Aug&nbsp;2007 | NA (correct) |
| a look-alike hyphen inside the upper number ("3&#8209;3/4"; next slide) | 9 | 13&nbsp;Dec&nbsp;2017 to 29&nbsp;Apr&nbsp;2026 | NA |
| a look-alike hyphen inside the lower number ("1&#8209;1/2"; next slide) | 3 | 11&nbsp;Dec&nbsp;2019, 29&nbsp;Jan&nbsp;2020, 15&nbsp;Jun&nbsp;2022 | 1.75 to 1.75;<br>FRED: 1.5 to 1.75 |
| "decided" is first about asset purchases, so the match runs on (up to 2,354 characters, across paragraphs) to the first "to 1/4 percent" | 6 | 19&nbsp;Mar to 29&nbsp;Oct&nbsp;2014 | 0.25 to 0.25;<br>FRED: 0 to 0.25 |

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The 2014 segments run 2,330 to 2,354 characters with two paragraph
breaks, except 29 Oct 2014 (851 characters). In these statements "federal
funds rate" follows the range, so the first "to X percent" in the
stretch is "to 1/4 percent". The reply's explanation quotes "by 1/2
percentage point, to 1 to 1-1/4 percent" as a phrase it handles; that is
3 Mar 2020, written with the look-alike hyphen, so that row is NA.
:::

:::

## Two hyphens that look the same {#hyphens .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc, seg and num from chat_reply.R"
j <- which(fomc$date == "2025-12-10")
str_view(seg[j], num)
utf8ToInt(str_extract(seg[j], "3.3/4"))     # . matches either hyphen; utf8ToInt(): each code point
utf8ToInt("3-3/4")                           # typed with the hyphen key
sum(str_detect(fomc$text, "\u2011"))         # statements with character 8209
```

::: {style="font-size:0.66em"}

In the `str_view()` output, "3-1/2" is one match but "3&#8209;3/4" is two,
`<3>` and `<3/4>`: `num` stops at the look-alike hyphen, so the row is NA.

:::

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](figures/16-text-regex/D08-two-hyphens.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Two versions of 3-3/4 side by side that look the same: one typed with the hyphen key, character 45, and one from the Fed's web pages, character 8209, the non-breaking hyphen."}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.66em"}

- **Code point**: the number a computer stores for each character.
  Unicode is the standard list of them.
- **Character 8209**: a non-breaking hyphen. Web pages use it to keep
  "3&#8209;3/4" on one line. In R, `"\u2011"` writes it: 2011 is 8209 in
  hexadecimal (base 16), the form Unicode lists use.
- The `-` in a pattern matches only character 45.

:::

:::

:::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The Fed's pages use character 8209 fifty times, in 34 statements from
July 2015 on, and in 12 of them it sits inside a number.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

**Characters and encodings.** A file stores each character as bytes, and
an encoding is the rule that turns bytes back into characters. UTF-8 is
the rule the statements file uses and the default in current R. Read with
the wrong rule, the same bytes give different characters: reading the file
with `read.csv("fomc_statements.csv", fileEncoding = "CP1252")` turns
"Today’s" into "Todayâ€™s". The fix is to read the file again with the
right rule (`encoding = "UTF-8"`), which gives the text back exactly;
converting the damaged text back with `iconv()` does not restore every
character.

:::

## Fixing the reply's code {#fixes .smaller}

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc, num, to_num() and the FRED columns"
# 1. the look-alike hyphen (character 8209) becomes "-"
fomc$text <- str_replace_all(fomc$text, "\u2011", "-")
# 2. stop at the period; 3. three verbs, no "federal funds rate"
seg <- str_extract(fomc$text, regex("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b",
                                    ignore_case = TRUE))
# 3. no "to/at/of" before the number
m <- str_match(seg, str_c("(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b"))
fomc$lower <- to_num(m[, 2])
fomc$upper <- ifelse(is.na(m[, 3]), fomc$lower, to_num(m[, 3]))
fomc$agree <- fomc$lower == fomc$fred_lower & fomc$upper == fomc$fred_upper
table(fomc$agree, useNA = "ifany")
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.72em"}

- **Change 1**: every look-alike hyphen (character 8209) becomes "-".
  This fixes the 12 hyphen rows.
- **Change 2**: `[^.]*?`, as few characters as possible that are not a
  period, replaces `.*?`, and `dotall` goes. Inside brackets the dot is a
  plain period, so the match ends with its sentence. The six 2014 rows
  now give NA in place of a wrong number.
- **Change 3**: step 1 accepts "maintain" and "reaffirmed" and drops
  "federal funds rate", which can come after the number ("the current 0
  to 1/4 percent target range for the federal funds rate"). Step 2 drops
  "to|at|of", since "current 0 to 1/4" has none.

:::

## Results after each fix {#fix-table .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Each row adds one change to the rows above. Counted against FRED on the
day after each statement:

| Code | NA | Wrong | Equal |
|:------------------------------------|--:|--:|--:|
| The reply as given | 32 | 9 | 130 |
| 1. Replace the look-alike hyphen with "-" | 23 | 6 | 142 |
| 2. Keep the match in one sentence | 36 | 0 | 135 |
| 3. Accept "maintain" and "reaffirmed"; take the range wherever it sits in the sentence | 1 | 0 | 170 |

:::

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.8em"}

- Change 2 turns the six 2014 values into NA. It does the same to seven
  statements from Nov 2010 to Jan 2014, where "decided" is about asset
  purchases and the range sits in a later sentence. The old match reached
  it only by crossing sentences.
- The last NA is 17 Aug 2007, which states no target.
- To ask the chatbot for a fix, paste the failing sentences with FRED's
  numbers for each. They are known-answer tests.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The seven: 3 Nov 2010, 14 Dec 2010, 26 Jan 2011, 15 Mar 2011, 27 Apr
2011, 18 Dec 2013 and 29 Jan 2014. The code for the two middle rows is on
the page.
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

The two middle rows of the table, run on a fresh copy of the reply's
output:

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console, in the 16-text-regex folder; needs stringr; reads the files again"
#| purl: false
f <- read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")
f$text <- str_replace_all(f$text, "\u2011", "-")
k2 <- match(as.Date(f$date) + 1, as.Date(fred$date))
count_rows <- function(lo, up) {
  ag <- lo == fred$lower[k2] & up == fred$upper[k2]
  c(missing = sum(is.na(ag)), wrong = sum(ag %in% FALSE), equal = sum(ag %in% TRUE))
}
s1 <- str_extract(f$text, regex("decided.*?federal funds rate.*?percent\\b",
                                ignore_case = TRUE, dotall = TRUE))   # after change 1
m1 <- str_match(s1, pat)
count_rows(to_num(m1[, 2]), ifelse(is.na(m1[, 3]), to_num(m1[, 2]), to_num(m1[, 3])))
s2 <- str_extract(f$text, regex("decided[^.]*?federal funds rate[^.]*?percent\\b",
                                ignore_case = TRUE))                  # after change 2
m2 <- str_match(s2, pat)
count_rows(to_num(m2[, 2]), ifelse(is.na(m2[, 3]), to_num(m2[, 2]), to_num(m2[, 3])))
```

:::

# 6 · When to use regex {#part-miss}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

- When to use regex
- What net tone misses
- Practice

:::

## When to use regex {#when-regex .smaller}

::::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.86em"}

**Regex works well when**

- the text follows a format: IDs, dates, amounts, codes
- the wording repeats, as in the Fed's sentence that states the target
  range
- you can list the variants and test each one
- you need the same answer every time the code runs
- the corpus is large: a pattern runs on millions of documents in
  seconds, for free

:::

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.86em"}

**Use a parser or a model when**

- the meaning depends on context or on negation: the Fed's "might not be
  strong enough" (13 Sep 2012) scores as positive
- the same idea is written in more ways than you can list
- the text is a web page (HTML) or data from an API (JSON), where parts
  sit inside other parts
- the variable is a judgment call, such as whether a sentence signals
  that the Fed will raise its rate

:::

:::

:::::

::: {style="font-size:0.7em"}

**Parser**: a function that reads a structured format into its parts,
such as `jsonlite::fromJSON()` for JSON or `rvest::read_html()` for a web
page. **Model**: a language model, the kind of program behind a chatbot,
asked to read each text and return a label, or a statistical classifier
trained on texts that people labeled by hand.

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.76em"}

A pattern gives NA or a wrong number, with no error message, when the
wording or a character changes. A chatbot can write the pattern. You still
read it, test it on strings from your documents, and compare its output
with a second source such as FRED.

:::

## What net tone misses {#miss .smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

The target range has a second source, FRED, and 170 of 171 values now
equal it. Net tone has no second source, so its errors show only when you
read the sentences it scored. The finance word list scores each word on
its own:

:::

```{r}
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc"
s <- str_extract(fomc$text[fomc$date == "2012-09-13"], "economic growth might not[^.]*")
str_view(s, "\\b(not|strong|improvement)\\b")
```

::: {.dashes style="font-size:0.76em"}

- **Negation.** 13 Sep 2012 (also 24 Oct and 12 Dec 2012): "strong" and
  "improvement" count as positive. Each word is scored on its own, so the
  "not" before them changes nothing.
- **Context.** 25 Apr 2012, "the unemployment rate has declined but
  remains elevated": "unemployment" and "declined" count as negative,
  although a falling unemployment rate is good news.
- **The event behind the words.** 3 Mar 2020, a cut in the target range
  between scheduled meetings as the coronavirus spread, is the 8th most
  positive of 171 statements. "strong", "achieving" and "stability" count
  as positive. "coronavirus" and "risks" are on neither list.

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The full 13 Sep 2012 sentence opens "The Committee is concerned that",
and "concerned" is on the negative list, so the sentence nets +1. Shapiro
and Wilson ignored words after "not", ran their estimates without
"unemployment", and filtered phrases such as "price stability"; their
estimates barely moved (working paper version).
:::

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

**Words the finance list misreads in Fed statements.**


::: {style="font-size:0.74em"}

| Word | List | Times | In a Fed statement |
|:--|:--|--:|:---------------------------|
| unemployment | negative | 154 | a statistic: "unemployment rate" (141) |
| against | negative | 86 | the vote: "Voting against" (75) |
| impede | negative | 46 | one set phrase about risks to the committee's goals |
| declined | negative | 45 | good news in "the unemployment rate declined" (18 statements) |
| stability | positive | 223 | the goal: "price stability" (218) |
| exceptionally | positive | 56 | always "exceptionally low", about the rate |

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.74em"}

Dropping unemployment, against, stability and exceptionally leaves the
lowest statement unchanged and makes 12 Jun 2024 the highest (Practice 8).

:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.notes}
The impede phrase is "if risks emerge that could impede the attainment of
the Committee's goals", 45 times with a straight apostrophe and once with
a curly one.
:::

:::


:::

## Practice {#practice .smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

Ten exercises on the session page, with solutions behind a click. Run
them after the slides' code, which builds `fomc`, `tokens`, `pos` and
`neg` from the files in the 16-text-regex folder. None needs an internet
connection.

- **1–4** Patterns and numbers: the opening phrase by year; rate moves
  stated in basis points (1 basis point = 0.01 percentage point), and
  which come from members who voted against; the vote, such as "12 – 0",
  in the 2026 statements; validating the web address (url) of each
  statement
- **5** Base R: the three fixes to the chatbot's code, rewritten with
  `gsub()`, `regmatches()` and `regexec()`
- **6–7** Word counts: "inflation" as a share of tokens by year; the
  three word lists of
  [Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024)
  on the statements
- **8–9** Net tone: recomputed without unemployment, against, stability
  and exceptionally; the word after each "not"
- **10** Characters: every character with a code point above 127, such as
  the dash in "12 – 0"

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

Task 7 uses the word lists of
[Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024).

```{r}
#| label: practice
#| exercise: true
#| script: "Practice"
#| eval: false
# Practice. Run in the 16-text-regex folder with stringr loaded, after the
# slides' code has built fomc (with the three changes), tokens, pos, neg
# and the FRED columns.

# Patterns and numbers
#  1. Label each statement by its opening with ^: "Information received",
#     "Recent indicators", or "other". Count them by year with table().
#  2. Run str_match(fomc$text, "(\\d+) basis points") and table() column 2.
#     Read each matching sentence. Which matches are not the committee's
#     decision? Change the pattern so only decisions match.
#  3. The 2026 statements give the vote ("by a 12 – 0 vote"). Extract the
#     two numbers as numeric columns. Why does "by a (\\d+) - (\\d+) vote"
#     fail? Use utf8ToInt() on the character between the numbers.
#  4. Validate the url column: every address should look like
#     https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetaryYYYYMMDDa.htm
#     Write the pattern with ^, \d{8} and $. Which addresses fail, and why?
# Base R
#  5. Rewrite the three changes with gsub(), regmatches() with regexpr(),
#     and regexec(). Do the same 170 statements equal FRED?
# Word counts
#  6. For each statement, compute the share of its tokens that are
#     "inflation". Average it by year with tapply(share, fomc$year, mean),
#     which applies mean() within each year, and plot it. Which year is
#     highest, which lowest?
#  7. Apply the core words of the three lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis
#     (QJE, 2016) to the statements with \\b and |. How many statements
#     match each list, and all three, and in which years?
# Tone
#  8. Recompute net tone after removing "unemployment" and "against" from
#     neg, and "stability" and "exceptionally" from pos. Which statements
#     are now lowest and highest? Where does 3 Mar 2020 land?
#  9. List the word after every "not" with str_match_all(), which returns
#     str_match()'s matrix for every match in each statement. How many are
#     on the positive list, and how many on the negative list?
# Characters
# 10. List every character with a code point above 127, with its code
#     point, its count, and the statements it appears in. Which would you
#     replace before matching?
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"}

```{r}
#| label: practice-solutions
#| purl: false
#| filename: "R Console; needs fomc, tokens, pos, neg, num, to_num() and fred"
# 1. Openings by year
op <- ifelse(str_detect(fomc$text, "^Information received"), "Information received",
      ifelse(str_detect(fomc$text, "^Recent indicators"), "Recent indicators", "other"))
table(op)
table(fomc$year, op)[c("2009", "2019", "2020", "2022", "2026"), ]
# 2. Basis points: 20 matches, 7 of them in dissents
bp <- str_match(fomc$text, "(\\d+) basis points")
table(bp[, 2])
dec <- str_match(fomc$text, "decided[^.]*?(\\d+) basis points")
table(dec[, 2])
# 3. The vote: the character between the numbers is an en dash, 8211
vt <- str_match(fomc$text, "by a (\\d+) (.) (\\d+) vote")
vt[!is.na(vt[, 1]), ]
utf8ToInt(vt[!is.na(vt[, 1]), 3][1])
# 4. Statement addresses: three end in "b.htm", a second release that day
url_ok <- str_detect(fomc$url,
  "^https://www\\.federalreserve\\.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary\\d{8}a\\.htm$")
fomc$url[!url_ok]
# 5. The three changes in base R
tx  <- gsub("\u2011", "-", fomc$text)
sg  <- regmatches(tx, regexpr("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b", tx,
                              ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE))
has <- grepl("(?:decided|maintain|reaffirmed)[^.]*?percent\\b", tx,
             ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
seg_b <- rep(NA_character_, length(tx))
seg_b[has] <- sg
mb <- regmatches(seg_b, regexec(paste0("(", num, ")(?:\\s+to\\s+(", num, "))?\\s+percent\\b"),
                                seg_b, perl = TRUE))
lo <- sapply(mb, function(v) if (length(v)) to_num(v[2]) else NA)
hi <- sapply(mb, function(v) if (length(v) && v[3] != "") to_num(v[3]) else NA)
hi <- ifelse(is.na(hi), lo, hi)
table(lo == fomc$fred_lower & hi == fomc$fred_upper, useNA = "ifany")
# 6. "inflation" as a share of tokens, by year
share <- sapply(tokens, function(w) mean(w == "inflation"))
by_year <- tapply(share, fomc$year, mean)
round(100 * by_year[c(which.max(by_year), which.min(by_year))], 2)
plot(as.numeric(names(by_year)), 100 * by_year, type = "b", xlab = "",
     ylab = "\"inflation\", percent of tokens", las = 1)
# 7. The three word lists of Baker, Bloom & Davis
E <- str_detect(fomc$text, regex("\\beconom(y|ic)\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))
U <- str_detect(fomc$text, regex("\\buncertain(ty)?\\b", ignore_case = TRUE))
P <- str_detect(fomc$text, "\\b(Congress|deficit|Federal Reserve|legislation|regulation|White House)\\b")
c(economy = sum(E), uncertainty = sum(U), policy = sum(P), all_three = sum(E & U & P))
table(fomc$year[E & U & P])
# 8. Tone without the four misread words
pos2 <- setdiff(pos, c("stability", "exceptionally"))
neg2 <- setdiff(neg, c("unemployment", "against"))
tone2 <- sapply(tokens, function(w) 100 * (sum(w %in% pos2) - sum(w %in% neg2)) / length(w))
round(cor(fomc$tone, tone2), 2)
fomc$date[c(which.min(tone2), which.max(tone2))]
match(which(fomc$date == "2020-03-03"), order(-tone2))     # its rank, most positive first
# 9. The word after "not"
nm <- str_match_all(str_to_lower(fomc$text), "\\bnot ([a-z]+)")
after_not <- unlist(lapply(nm, function(x) x[, 2]))
length(after_not)
c(positive = sum(after_not %in% pos), negative = sum(after_not %in% neg))
# 10. Characters above code point 127
ch <- unlist(strsplit(read.csv("fomc_statements.csv")$text, ""))
odd <- ch[sapply(ch, utf8ToInt) > 127]
sort(table(sapply(odd, utf8ToInt)), decreasing = TRUE)
```

## Quick reference {#reference}

**Pattern pieces:** `.` any character · `\\.` a period · `\\d` a digit ·
`\\s` a space or line break · `[ ]` one of a set · `[^ ]` one not in the
set · `+` one or more · `*` zero or more · `?` zero or one · `{n}` exactly
n · `.*?` as few as possible · `^` start · `$` end · `\\b` a word boundary
· `( )` a capture group · `(?: )` a group with no column · `|` either
side · `regex(p, ignore_case = TRUE, dotall = TRUE)`.

**Functions:** `str_detect`, `str_count`, `str_view`, `str_extract`,
`str_extract_all`, `str_match`, `str_replace_all`, `str_sub`, `str_c`,
`str_to_lower`, `regex`, `utf8ToInt`, `match`, `table`, `sort`, `unlist`,
`which`, `is.na`, `%in%`, `sapply`, `which.min`, `which.max`.

**The word list.** The shipped file keeps the words whose Positive or
Negative flag in the master dictionary is a year above 0, because a
negative year marks a word removed from the list. It leaves out 17
removed words, so it has 347 positive and 2,345 negative words; Shapiro
and Wilson used an earlier version. The master dictionary has five more
lists (uncertainty, litigious, strong modal, weak modal, constraining).

**Sources.**
[Baker, Bloom & Davis (QJE, 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw024);
[Shapiro & Wilson (REStud, 2022)](https://doi.org/10.1093/restud/rdab094),
"Taking the Fed at its Word: A New Approach to Estimating Central Bank
Objectives using Text Analysis" (method details from
[FRBSF Working Paper 2019-02](https://doi.org/10.24148/wp2019-02));
[Djourelova (AER, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20211537);
[Loughran & McDonald (JF, 2011)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2010.01625.x)
and their [master dictionary](https://sraf.nd.edu/loughranmcdonald-master-dictionary/).
FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis:
[DFEDTAR](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTAR),
[DFEDTARL](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARL),
[DFEDTARU](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU).
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, federalreserve.gov
(public domain; [disclaimer](https://www.federalreserve.gov/disclaimer.htm)).

The statements were collected from federalreserve.gov in October 2026,
FRED's series were downloaded the same month, and the word list is the
authors' March 2026 update.

[stringr](https://stringr.tidyverse.org) ·
[Syllabus](../syllabus.qmd)
